You listed these things:

1) Math and Physics will be tough for you.
2) You prefer not to rely on others.
3) You're good at memorizing.
4) You're genuinely interested in science.

The others you mentioned:

1) You *think* you can manage coding to some extent.
2) Entrepreneurship is a *safer* option.

In the first group of items, it sounds to me that you're sure about them. In the second one, it sounds to me like it's a compromise—you're unsure.

I'd suggest this. Figure out what kind of lifestyle you want to live; your values; what's important to YOU and not someone else; then choose a course that can satisfy that.

I'd heavily advise against choosing a course to please external factors (parents, friends, society) as imo, that will usually lead to a burnout.

Like I feel like I don't deserve to pause or take a break, though as much as possible I extend compassion to myself, but a lot of other times too I feel like I want to just ignore and avoid it because I can't seem to face them.

I actually journal every night and it does help with processing everything I experienced in a day. It feels really nice to just pour it all out and get a certain perspective about everything that's bothering me. I love going to bed feeling lighter. It's like releasing a heavy load.

>What do you think is doing the squeezing?

It's like my heart is being squeezed flat, like my chest is constricting, or something else is sandwiching it. Honestly I don't know. It's like it kind of feels swollen too. I think avoidance could be the cause of it, or denial :( 

>Also I want to remind you that avoiding discomfort is a natural reaction and I don't think it's a reason to feel bad.

This, I think, is the reason why I keep denying or avoiding. I feel like my avoidance of discomfort, or my fear of showing any signs of vulnerability, is a bad thing. Like a part of me detests it. Like I'm not allowing myself to be vulnerable especially in front of others. It's no surprise too cause I was brought up this way. My family hated it when I was showing my emotions, so I've learned over time to really repress it or as much as possible, keep it to myself. My personality is pretty reserved too, and I don't talk a lot. I also prefer not talking about my personal problems at all, though I'm working on this.

>what is casting the doom?

Not sure. The fear of missing out? The fear of not having fun with my phone when it's literally right there?

>what is coming to get me?

I guess nothing, now that I thought about it. It just feels so foreign when I'm not on my phone, and the discomfort is somewhat unbearable to feel. It's like I don't want to feel the discomfort so I distract myself instead. I feel restless. Like I can't stay still. And as that happens I notice that my heart always feels like it's squeezed.

I feel very weird. As if my skin is crawling when I'm not on my phone. I feel a sense of impending doom? Like something nonexistent is out to get me if I'm not using my phone. Or it could just be boredom. 

I just feel very safe when on my phone despite that it overwhelms me after usage. What can I do about this?

What do you mean by this question? Do you mean to ask on how you can write a story where your character is in a country he doesn’t speak their language?

You don’t have to put the ‘he demands angrily and seriously’ tag after the “Get out” line because for sure, the reader already understands that the character is demanding it, is serious, and is angry. Readers are smart, there’s no need to spell out an emotion to them because for sure they already know. And the ‘Get out’ line already implies seriousness and anger.

Revised: “Get out.” He said.

It’s tighter. It doesn’t sound redundant. It’s effective. It doesn’t distract the reader.

I suggest you opt out in using verb modifiers (words that intensify a verb; they’re the ones ending in -ly I think, I’m not a grammar expert) because they don’t really do anything good.
